lessons.title: der Vater, die Mutter — the family that proves Grimm's law
lessons.gloss: father and mother — Grimm's law makes them twins of English father/mother

segments.text: Back in the months chapter, German borrowed its calendar from Latin (Januar, März…). Family is the opposite story: Vater and Mutter are not borrowed — they are inherited Germanic words, blood cousins of English father and mother. And the sound-law that links them, Grimm's law, is written right on their faces.
der Vater ("father") — note the spelling V, but it is pronounced f (FAH-ter). from PIE ph₂tḗr.
Grimm's law is the great sound-shift that split the Germanic languages (English, German, Dutch…) off from the rest. Watch what it did to the same PIE words that Latin kept as pater/māter:

utterances: PIE: ph₂tḗr. Latin (French): pater (père). Germanic (English / German): father / Vater (V = f).
PIE: méh₂tēr. Latin (French): māter (mère). Germanic (English / German): mother / Mutter.

segments.text: p becomes f: Latin kept the p (pater); Germanic turned it to f — English father, German Vater (the V is just an old spelling of that f sound).
t becomes th becomes d: the middle consonant became English th (mother) and then, in German's later shift, d/t (Mutter).

So German and English agree here (both f-, both m-) precisely because they are both Germanic — while French/Latin sit on the other side of Grimm's line. The month names were Latin tourists; Vater and Mutter are natives.

segments.instruction: "der Vater, die Mutter" — Vater with an f sound
segments.source: [YOU SAY: "der Vater, die Mutter" — *Vater* with an **f** sound]

segments.instruction: the twin test — "Vater / father, Mutter / mother — both Germanic"

segments.instruction: contrast — "German months = Latin (Januar); German family = Germanic (Vater)"
segments.source: [YOU SAY: contrast — "German months = Latin (Januar); German family = Germanic (Vater)"]

segments.text: Give "father" and "mother" with articles, minding the pronunciation. (der Vater — f sound — die Mutter.) Why do German Vater and English father match, while French père differs? (German & English are both Germanic — Grimm's law shifted p becomes f in both; French kept Latin's p.) How does this chapter contrast with the months chapter? (Months were borrowed from Latin; family is inherited Germanic.) Next: Bruder and Schwester.

lessons.title: der Bruder, die Schwester — and the word for "siblings"
lessons.gloss: brother and sister — again Germanic twins of the English words

segments.text: The parent pair proved German and English are Germanic twins. The sibling pair does it again: Bruder ("brother") and Schwester ("sister") are the near-identical cousins of the English words — no translation really needed, just an ear for the German sounds.
der Bruder ("brother") from PIE bʰréh₂tēr — the same root as Latin frāter (French frère), but here kept with a b- (Grimm's law changed bʰ becomes b), exactly like English brother.
die Schwester ("sister") from PIE swésōr. The German sch spells an sh sound; strip it back and Schwester is English sister and Latin soror, all one root.

German has a tidy word English lacks: die Geschwister = "siblings," brothers-and-sisters together. It is built with the ge- prefix, an old collective marker ("a set of…") on Schwester — the same ge- that bundles mountains into a Gebirge ("range") and lets German gather a family in one word.
The four family words now stand as a Germanic set beside the Romance ones:

utterances: German: Vater / Mutter. English: father / mother. (Romance cousin): père / mère.
German: Bruder / Schwester. English: brother / sister. (Romance cousin): frère / sœur.

segments.instruction: the twin test — "Bruder / brother, Schwester / sister"
"die Geschwister — the ge- bundles them into 'siblings'"
segments.source: [YOU SAY: "die Geschwister — the *ge-* bundles them into 'siblings'"]

segments.text: Give "brother" and "sister" with articles. (der Bruder, die Schwester.) Why do they match English so closely? (Both Germanic — same PIE roots, no Grimm's-law gap between them.) What does Geschwister mean, and what does the ge- do? ("Siblings"; ge- is a collective prefix, "a set of.") Next chapter: putting the family into sentences.
